newsitem.title: USA: U.S. women deserve credit for growing clout - study.
newsitem.headline: U.S. women deserve credit for growing clout - study.

text.p: U.S. women, who helped vote President Clinton back into office, have not been given due credit for their growing economic and political clout, feminists and researchers said Tuesday.

"The degree to which women have empowered themselves to a position of near-equality to men has not been sufficiently recognised by the president, by the leaders of the Democratic or Republican parties or by the CEOs of this country," feminist author Betty Friedan said.

"And they had better get with it," Friedan said at a news conference to announce results of research on U.S. women's political and economic status and their ability to exercise reproductive rights in all 50 states and Washington, D.C.

Friedan and others at the briefing pointed to political polling that showed a pro-Clinton gender gap in the presidential race and indicated that if only men had voted Clinton might have lost the Nov. 5 election.
Women's apparent ability to swing elections does not translate into economic power or higher pay, however, according to data analysed by the Washington-based Institute for Women's Policy Research.

"Women aren't in the driver's seat anywhere in America, but we've made it to the front of the bus in some states while we're still running to catch the bus in some other states," said Heidi Hartmann, who heads the institute.

For example, the institute's figures showed that women's average salaries did not outpace men's anywhere in the United States. The narrowest wage gap was in Washington, where women earned nearly 88 cents for every dollar men made. The widest gap was in West Virginia, where women earned less than 59 cents for every dollar men were paid.

The wage gap narrowed over the decade 1980-1990, researchers said, largely due to an overall decline in men's salaries. While the median annual earnings for women increased by 8.4 percent, men's fell by 9.0 percent for the same period.

In terms of women's political participation, the top five states were Kansas, Washington state, Minnesota, Maine and Maryland. The lowest-ranked states were Tennessee, Kentucky, Mississippi, Pennsylvania and Arkansas.
Women did best economically in Washington, D.C., Alaska, Maryland, Massachusetts and Connecticut; they were worst off in West Virginia, Mississippi, Kentucky, Alabama, Arkansas and Indiana.

Overall, women's status was lowest in the southern states, with Mississippi, Kentucky, Arkansas and Tennessee ranking among the bottom 10 for political participation, earnings, economic autonomy and reproductive rights.
